title: Grade 12 Chemistry — Coordination Compounds
description: IUPAC nomenclature, bonding theories, isomerism, and applications
subject: chemistry

questions.question: A coordination compound consists of a:
options: Metal ion bonded to covalently bonded molecules only
Central metal atom/ion surrounded by ligands (Lewis bases donating electron pairs)
Metal atom directly bonded to another metal
questions.explanation: Coordination compound: central metal atom/ion surrounded by ligands (molecules or ions donating electron pairs to the metal). Example: [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻ — Fe²⁺ is the centre; CN⁻ are ligands.

questions.question: Ligands are classified by the number of donor atoms. A bidentate ligand has:
options: Two donor atoms that can simultaneously bond to the metal (e.g., en = ethylenediamine, oxalate)
questions.explanation: Bidentate: two donor atoms (e.g., ethylenediamine H₂N−CH₂−CH₂−NH₂; oxalate C₂O₄²⁻). Monodentate: one donor (Cl⁻, H₂O, NH₃). Polydentate (chelate): ≥3 donors. EDTA is hexadentate.

questions.question: The IUPAC name of [Co(NH₃)₅Cl]²⁺ is:
questions.explanation: IUPAC: ligands named first (alphabetically), then metal with oxidation state in Roman numerals. Ligands: 5 NH₃ (pentaammine) + 1 Cl (chlorido). Co charge: total complex = +2, Cl = −1, NH₃ = 0 → Co = +3. Name: pentaamminechloridocobalt(III).

questions.question: Werner's coordination theory established that coordination compounds have:
options: Both primary valence (ionisation valence) and secondary valence (coordination number)
questions.explanation: Werner: metal ions have (1) primary valence = ionic valence/oxidation state (satisfied by anions); (2) secondary valence = coordination number (satisfied by ligands around the metal). Fixed, directional. Nobel Prize 1913.

questions.question: The coordination number of Fe in [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻ is:
questions.explanation: Coordination number = number of bonds from ligands to the central metal. [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻: 6 CN⁻ ligands each bonded through C → coordination number = 6. Fe oxidation state: overall −4, 6×(−1) = −6 from CN⁻ → Fe = +2.

questions.question: Ionisation isomerism occurs in coordination compounds when:
options: Two compounds have the same formula but different spatial arrangements
Ligands inside and outside the coordination sphere exchange, giving different ions in solution
A chelate ring is formed differently
The metal has different oxidation states
questions.explanation: Ionisation isomers: same formula, but differ in which groups are inside/outside the coordination sphere. Example: [Co(NH₃)₅Br]SO₄ (gives SO₄²⁻ in solution) vs. [Co(NH₃)₅SO₄]Br (gives Br⁻ in solution).

questions.question: Crystal Field Theory explains the colour of coordination compounds by:
options: Electronic transitions between metal and ligand orbitals
Splitting of d orbitals due to ligand field → d-d transitions absorb visible light
Ionic bond formation between metal and ligand
Covalent bond breaking in the complex
questions.explanation: Crystal Field Theory (CFT): ligands exert an electrostatic field that splits d orbitals into two sets (e.g., t₂g and eg in octahedral). Electrons absorb visible light for d-d transitions; complementary colour is observed.

questions.question: Geometrical (cis-trans) isomerism in coordination compounds requires:
options: The same coordination number but different shapes
Same formula with ligands arranged differently in space — not interconvertible without breaking bonds
questions.explanation: Geometrical isomerism: same formula, different spatial arrangement of ligands. Example: cis-[Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] (Cl groups on same side) vs. trans-[Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] (Cl groups on opposite sides). Cisplatin (cis isomer) is an anticancer drug.

questions.question: The effective atomic number (EAN) rule predicts stable complexes when the total electron count around the metal equals:
questions.explanation: 18-electron rule (EAN/Sidgwick rule): stable transition metal complexes often have 18 electrons around the metal. Example: [Fe(CO)₅]: Fe(0) has 8e⁻ + 5×CO(2e⁻ each) = 18e⁻. Applies mainly to organometallic compounds.

questions.question: Chelate complexes are more stable than corresponding non-chelate complexes due to:
options: Chelate effect — entropy gain when polydentate ligand displaces multiple monodentate ligands
questions.explanation: Chelate effect: when a polydentate ligand (e.g., EDTA) replaces monodentate ligands, the number of free molecules increases → entropy increases → ΔG becomes more negative → greater stability. EDTA forms very stable chelates with metal ions.

questions.question: Haemoglobin is a coordination compound where the central metal ion is:
options: Fe²⁺ in a porphyrin ring that binds O₂ reversibly
questions.explanation: Haemoglobin: Fe²⁺ in a porphyrin (haem) group binds O₂ reversibly. In lungs: Fe²⁺−O₂ formed (oxyhaemoglobin). In tissues: O₂ released (deoxyhaemoglobin). CO binds much more strongly than O₂ (carboxyhaemoglobin = toxic).

questions.question: The IUPAC name of [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺ is:
questions.explanation: 4 NH₃ ligands = tetraammine (no space); Cu²⁺ = copper(II). Complex cation: [tetraammine][copper(II)] ion. Not 'cuprate' (that's for complex anions). Charge: 4×0 + Cu = +2.

questions.question: Spectrochemical series ranks ligands by their ability to split d orbitals. Which is a STRONG field ligand?
questions.explanation: Spectrochemical series (weak → strong): I⁻ < Br⁻ < S²⁻ < Cl⁻ < F⁻ < OH⁻ < H₂O < NH₃ < en < CN⁻ < CO. Strong field → large splitting → low-spin complex (electrons pair). Weak field → small splitting → high-spin.

questions.question: Optical isomers (enantiomers) of coordination compounds are non-superimposable mirror images. They are observed mainly in:
options: Octahedral complexes with bidentate or mixed ligands (e.g., [Co(en)₃]³⁺)
questions.explanation: Optical isomerism: most common in octahedral complexes with bidentate ligands. [Co(en)₃]³⁺ (tris-ethylenediamine cobalt) exists as Δ (delta) and Λ (lambda) enantiomers. They rotate plane-polarised light in opposite directions.

questions.question: Cisplatin [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] is used as an anticancer drug because:
options: It is highly toxic and kills all cells
The cis isomer binds to DNA strands, preventing cell division in cancer cells
It is the trans isomer that is medically useful
questions.explanation: Cisplatin (cis-[Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂]) is an anticancer drug: the cis arrangement allows it to crosslink two guanine bases on the same DNA strand, blocking replication. The trans isomer is NOT biologically active. Used for testicular, ovarian, bladder cancers.
